title: Save More Tomorrow
text:
Many people know they should save more for retirement and still do not. Richard Thaler and Shlomo Benartzi designed a program around the reasons: people put off unpleasant changes, and they hate seeing their take-home pay go down.

Their plan, called Save More Tomorrow, asked employees to commit now to raising their savings rate later, and to tie each increase to a future pay raise. Because the extra saving started only when a raise arrived, paychecks never shrank. The increases continued automatically with each raise until a ceiling was reached, and anyone could leave the program at any time.

The first test took place in the late 1990s at a midsize manufacturing company in the United States. Employees first met a financial consultant. Those who declined his advice to raise their savings immediately were offered Save More Tomorrow, and most of them accepted. Very few dropped out later. Over about three and a half years and four raises, participants' average savings rate rose from about 3.5 percent of pay to more than 13 percent, overtaking even the employees who had followed the consultant's advice right away.

Thaler and Benartzi published the results in 2004. The idea was adopted by many employers, and automatic escalation of contributions became a common feature of retirement plans.
lesson: If a good change is hard to start today, commit now to start it at a specific future moment, ideally one when it will hurt less, and let it happen automatically.
source: Thaler, R. H., and Benartzi, S. (2004). Save More Tomorrow: Using behavioral economics to increase employee saving. Journal of Political Economy, 112(S1), S164-S187.
